questions.question: Which structure covers the glottis during swallowing and so prevents food from entering the larynx?

solution.key_concept: The epiglottis is a cartilaginous flap that closes the glottis during swallowing.
steps: The pharynx is the common passage for food and air.
During swallowing, the epiglottis covers the glottis, so food is directed away from the larynx.
solution.why_not_others: The larynx is the cartilaginous sound box. The pleura covers the lungs. The diaphragm forms the floor of the thoracic chamber.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the larynx (the sound box) with the epiglottis (the flap that guards the glottis).

questions.question: At the level of which vertebra does the human trachea divide into the right and left primary bronchi?

solution.key_concept: The trachea bifurcates into the two primary bronchi at the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra.
steps: The trachea runs down through the thoracic cavity.
It divides into the right and left primary bronchi at the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra.
solution.why_not_others: The 3rd thoracic and 7th cervical vertebrae lie too high. The lumbar vertebrae lie below the thorax.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the vertebra number or the vertebral region.

questions.question: Which of the following belongs to the respiratory or exchange part of the human respiratory system?

solution.key_concept: The conducting part runs from the nostrils to the terminal bronchioles. The alveoli and their ducts form the exchange part.
steps: The trachea, the bronchi and the terminal bronchioles only conduct air.
The alveoli and alveolar ducts form the respiratory or exchange part.
solution.why_not_others: Terminal bronchioles are the last segment of the conducting part. The tertiary bronchi and trachea are also conducting structures.
solution.common_trap: Assuming the terminal bronchioles take part in gas exchange because they are the last branches before the alveoli.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Human lungs are situated in an air-tight thoracic chamber.
statements.R: The pleural fluid between the two layers of pleura reduces friction on the lung surface.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: The air-tight thorax and the pleural fluid are separate features of lung anatomy.
steps: A is true: the lungs lie in an air-tight thoracic chamber.
R is true: the pleural fluid reduces friction.
Reducing friction does not explain why the chamber is air-tight, so R does not explain A.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are factually correct, so options 3 and 4 are ruled out. R is unrelated to the air-tightness described in A, so option 1 is wrong.
solution.common_trap: Linking any two true pleura or thorax facts as cause and effect.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: The trachea, the primary, secondary and tertiary bronchi and the initial bronchioles are supported by incomplete cartilaginous rings.
statements.II: The conducting part of the respiratory system extends from the external nostrils to the alveolar ducts and is the site of gas exchange.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Cartilaginous support of the airways, and the boundary between the conducting and exchange parts.
steps: Statement I is correct: these airways are supported by incomplete cartilaginous rings.
The conducting part ends at the terminal bronchioles.
The conducting part only filters, humidifies and warms air, and does not exchange gases.
So Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement II misplaces the end of the conducting part and gives it an exchange role.
solution.common_trap: Including the alveolar ducts in the conducting part.

questions.question: On average, a healthy human breathes how many times per minute?

solution.key_concept: The normal breathing rate of a healthy human is 12-16 per minute.
steps: A healthy human breathes 12 to 16 times per minute.
solution.why_not_others: 6-8 is too low and 20-25 is too high. 70-75 is the heart rate.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the breathing rate with the heart beat rate.

questions.question: Which centre moderates the respiratory rhythm by reducing the duration of inspiration and altering the respiratory rate?
options: Respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla
Chemosensitive area adjacent to the rhythm centre

solution.key_concept: The pneumotaxic centre in the pons moderates the rhythm set by the medullary centre.
steps: The medullary rhythm centre sets the basic rhythm.
The pneumotaxic centre in the pons shortens inspiration and alters the rate.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Pneumotaxic centre in the pons
solution.why_not_others: The rhythm centre sets the rhythm but does not moderate it. The chemosensitive area and the aortic arch receptors sense $CO_2$ and $H^+$.
solution.common_trap: Placing the pneumotaxic centre in the medulla, or confusing it with the rhythm centre.

questions.question: A healthy person has a tidal volume of 500 mL and breathes 14 times per minute. What is the volume of air inspired per minute?

solution.key_concept: Minute ventilation is tidal volume multiplied by the breathing rate.
steps: Use $V_{min} = TV \times f$.
solution.why_not_others: 514 mL comes from adding instead of multiplying. 3500 mL comes from halving the rate. 6000 mL uses a rate of 12 instead of 14.
solution.common_trap: Using the textbook rate of 12 instead of the rate given in the question.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_II.label: I
list_II.text: Increase in thoracic volume in the antero-posterior axis

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: Increase in thoracic volume in the dorso-ventral axis

solution.key_concept: Each inspiratory muscle enlarges the thorax along a specific axis, and each regulatory centre has a specific location and role.
steps: The diaphragm enlarges the thorax in the antero-posterior axis: A-I.
The external intercostals lift the ribs and sternum, enlarging the dorso-ventral axis: B-II.
The pneumotaxic centre lies in the pons: C-III.
The chemosensitive area senses $CO_2$ and $H^+$: D-IV.
solution.why_not_others: The other options swap the two axes, or swap the functions of the two centres.
solution.common_trap: Interchanging the antero-posterior and dorso-ventral axes.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the mechanism and regulation of breathing are correct?

statements.A: Normal expiration is passive and occurs by relaxation of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles.
statements.B: During inspiration the intra-pulmonary pressure becomes higher than the atmospheric pressure.
statements.C: Receptors in the aortic arch and carotid artery can recognise changes in $CO_2$ and $H^+$ concentration.
statements.D: Oxygen plays a major role in the regulation of the respiratory rhythm.
statements.E: Abdominal muscles can increase the strength of breathing.

solution.key_concept: Pressure changes during the breathing cycle, and the chemical regulation of breathing.
steps: A is true: normal expiration is passive.
B is false: during inspiration the intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric pressure.
C is true: the aortic arch and carotid receptors detect $CO_2$ and $H^+$.
D is false: oxygen has an insignificant role in regulation.
E is true: abdominal muscles can add force to breathing.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): A, C and E only
solution.why_not_others: Options 3 and 4 include the false statements B and/or D. Option 1 omits the true statement E.
solution.common_trap: Assuming oxygen is the main chemical regulator of breathing.

questions.question: What percentage of oxygen is transported by RBCs in the blood as oxyhaemoglobin?

solution.key_concept: Most of the $O_2$ in blood is carried bound to haemoglobin.
steps: About 97% of $O_2$ travels as oxyhaemoglobin in RBCs.
The remaining 3% is dissolved in plasma.
solution.why_not_others: 3% is the dissolved fraction of $O_2$. 7% and 70% are the dissolved and bicarbonate fractions of $CO_2$.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the $O_2$ transport percentages with the $CO_2$ transport percentages.

questions.question: A person has TV = 500 mL, IRV = 2500 mL, ERV = 1000 mL and RV = 1200 mL. What is the vital capacity?

solution.key_concept: Vital capacity is the sum of IRV, TV and ERV.
steps: Use $VC = IRV + TV + ERV$.
solution.why_not_others: 3000 mL is the inspiratory capacity (TV + IRV). 5200 mL is the total lung capacity (VC + RV). 2200 mL is the functional residual capacity (ERV + RV).
solution.common_trap: Adding the residual volume into the vital capacity.
solution.time_saving_tip: RV is never part of VC, because RV can never be expelled.

questions.question: Which set of conditions favours the formation of oxyhaemoglobin?
options: High $pO_2$, low $pCO_2$, low $H^+$ and lower temperature
Low $pO_2$, high $pCO_2$, high $H^+$ and higher temperature
High $pO_2$, high $pCO_2$, high $H^+$ and higher temperature
Low $pO_2$, low $pCO_2$, low $H^+$ and lower temperature

solution.key_concept: Conditions in the alveoli favour the binding of $O_2$ to haemoglobin.
steps: The alveoli have high $pO_2$, low $pCO_2$, low $H^+$ and lower temperature.
These conditions favour oxyhaemoglobin formation.
The reverse conditions, found in the tissues, favour dissociation.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): High $pO_2$, low $pCO_2$, low $H^+$ and lower temperature
solution.why_not_others: Option 2 describes tissue conditions, which favour dissociation. Options 3 and 4 mix favourable and unfavourable factors.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that higher temperature or higher $H^+$ helps $O_2$ binding.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: For the same difference in partial pressure, $CO_2$ diffuses across the alveolar membrane much more readily than $O_2$.
statements.R: The solubility of $CO_2$ is 20 to 25 times higher than that of $O_2$.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: The rate of diffusion depends on the solubility of the gas.
steps: Diffusion depends on the pressure gradient, the solubility of the gas and the membrane thickness.
$CO_2$ is 20 to 25 times more soluble than $O_2$.
Its higher solubility explains why it diffuses more readily per unit pressure difference.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are true, so options 3 and 4 are wrong. Solubility directly explains the diffusion difference, so option 2 is wrong.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that $CO_2$ diffuses poorly because its partial pressure gradient is small.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: The $pO_2$ of alveolar air (104 mm Hg) is higher than that of deoxygenated blood (40 mm Hg), so $O_2$ diffuses from the alveoli into the blood.
statements.II: About 70% of $CO_2$ is transported as bicarbonate, whose formation is catalysed by carbonic anhydrase.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Partial pressure gradients drive diffusion, and $CO_2$ is carried mainly as bicarbonate.
steps: The alveolar $pO_2$ is 104 mm Hg and the deoxygenated blood $pO_2$ is 40 mm Hg, so $O_2$ moves into the blood. Statement I is correct.
About 70% of $CO_2$ is carried as bicarbonate, formed with the help of carbonic anhydrase. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
solution.why_not_others: Both statements match the stated values and mechanisms.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the 70% bicarbonate share with the 20-25% carbamino-haemoglobin share.

questions.question: Emphysema is characterised by:
options: Damage to alveolar walls, which decreases the respiratory surface
Inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles, which causes wheezing
Fibrosis caused by inhaling silica dust
Proliferation of fibrous tissue caused by asbestos fibres

solution.key_concept: Emphysema is a chronic disorder in which the alveolar walls are damaged.
steps: In emphysema the alveolar walls are damaged.
As a result, the respiratory surface area decreases.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Damage to alveolar walls, which decreases the respiratory surface
solution.why_not_others: Option 2 describes asthma. Option 3 describes silicosis. Option 4 describes asbestosis.
solution.common_trap: Confusing emphysema with asthma.

questions.question: Difficulty in breathing with wheezing, caused by inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles, is characteristic of:

solution.key_concept: Asthma is caused by inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles.
steps: Wheezing together with inflamed bronchi and bronchioles indicates asthma.
solution.why_not_others: Emphysema involves damage to the alveolar walls. Silicosis and asbestosis are occupational fibrotic disorders caused by dust.
solution.common_trap: Choosing emphysema just because it is also a chronic breathing difficulty.

questions.question: Long exposure to dust in stone-breaking industries causes inflammation of the lungs. This inflammation leads to:

solution.key_concept: In occupational disorders, dust causes inflammation, which then leads to fibrosis.
steps: The dust overwhelms the body's defence mechanisms.
Long exposure causes inflammation, which leads to fibrosis (proliferation of fibrous tissue).
solution.why_not_others: Dust damage does not dilate the bronchioles or increase the alveolar surface. Thinning of the pleura is not a stated outcome.
solution.common_trap: Assuming the lung tissue thins out, when in fact fibrous tissue proliferates.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

solution.key_concept: Each respiratory disorder has a characteristic cause or lesion.
steps: Asthma: inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles, so A-II.
Emphysema: damaged alveolar walls, so B-IV.
Silicosis: silica dust, so C-III.
Asbestosis: asbestos fibres, so D-I.
solution.why_not_others: The other options swap asthma with emphysema, and/or swap silica with asbestos.
solution.common_trap: Interchanging the lesions of asthma and emphysema.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about respiratory disorders are correct?

statements.A: Asthma results from damage to the alveolar walls.
statements.B: Emphysema is a chronic disorder in which the respiratory surface decreases.
statements.C: Occupational respiratory disorders arise when the dust produced is so great that the body's defence mechanisms cannot cope.
statements.D: Fibrosis refers to the proliferation of fibrous tissue.
statements.E: Protective masks are of no value in preventing occupational respiratory disorders.

solution.key_concept: The features and prevention of asthma, emphysema and occupational disorders.
steps: A is false: asthma is inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles.
B is true: in emphysema the respiratory surface decreases.
C is true: occupational disorders arise when dust exceeds the body's defences.
D is true: fibrosis is the proliferation of fibrous tissue.
E is false: workers should wear protective masks.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): B, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Options 1, 2 and 3 each include the false statement A and/or E.
solution.common_trap: Attributing alveolar damage to asthma instead of emphysema.
